units.title: Livestock Production
units.intro:
Livestock = domesticated animals kept for food, work, fibre or income: cattle, sheep, goats, camels, donkeys, poultry (and a few others). Eritrea’s herd is mostly **extensive / pastoral–agro-pastoral** — animals walk to browse, with extra pressure in the dry season.

Book snapshot of national stock (order-of-magnitude): millions of sheep and goats, substantial cattle and camels, donkeys as the everyday transport animal, very few horses/mules, plus layers such as White Leghorn in more intensive pockets.

1.1.1 Definitions of Livestock and Farm Animals
body: **Livestock** is defined as “any creature kept for the production of food, wool, skins or fur, or for the purpose of its use in the farming of the land”.
Equines comprise horses, mules and donkeys.
Animal production, or animal husbandry, is the practice of raising animals to obtain products such as meat, milk, eggs, honey and fish (from ponds).
History of livestock: Humans began domesticating animals over 10 000 years ago, beginning with dogs.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Livestock Status and Population in Eritrea
body: In the six zobas of Eritrea, livestock play an important role in the livelihoods of the community and also constitute a key component of the agricultural productive system.
The majority of Eritrea’s livestock are indigenous.
The only exotic breeds introduced in significant numbers are the dairy breed of Holstein-Friesian cattle and the White Leghorn layer chickens.
Several thousand Large White pigs are, however, also found.

cards.title: 1.1.3 Values and Uses of Livestock
body: Livestock play a major role in Eritrean society.
Mixed farming systems where both crops and livestock are kept are common throughout Eritrea.
In these systems livestock are mainly used to plough the land where crops are grown and to provide manure for fertilizing the fields of crops.

cards.title: 1.1.4 Types and Classification of Livestock
body: Livestock are divided into different orders based on the number of toes or hooves they have.
Equines are hindgut fermenters and most digestion takes place in the caecum and the small intestine.
The Bovidae and Camelidae are foregut fermenters, with most digestion taking place in the rumen.
Pigs have a monogastric digestive system that is similar to that of humans.

cards.title: 1.1.5 Breeding and Breeds
body: **The caeca** are the sites for bacterial fermentation of undigested food material in most non-ruminant livestock.
**The colon** is the main site of water re-absorption.
**Breeding** is the mating of a male with a female to obtain a desired type of offspring or progeny.
The latter is called **artificial insemination**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The chemical process of cellulose digestion in ruminants is achieved by enzymes produced by which of the following?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Ruminant animals do not naturally produce cellulase, the enzyme required to digest cellulose. Cellulase is produced by the symbiotic bacteria, protozoa, and fungi residing within the rumen and reticulum.

**Conclusion**
Thus, cellulose digestion is achieved by **Rumen microorganisms**.

cards.title: Animal feeds and feeding
body: **Feeds:** roughages (hay, straw, browse) vs concentrates (grain, oil cake). A ration must cover energy, protein, minerals, vitamins and water — water first in Eritrea’s climate.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Feeds and Feed Composition
body: Feed (food) is a material, which, after ingestion by animals, is capable of being digested, absorbed and utilized.
Usually, the term “feed” is used to imply food for livestock.
Food contains materials that can be digested and that cannot be digested.
The components of the food that cannot be digested pass out of the body as faeces and urine.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Common Classifications and Types of Feeds
body: Feed refers to any non-injurious edible material with nutritional value and could be pasture, harvested forages, crop residues, grains or processed animal feeds.
Feeds that have low fibre content (less than 18 per cent) are termed **concentrates**.
Feeds that have high fibre content (more than 18 per cent) are termed **roughages**.
As the name indicates, concentrates are dense, whereas roughages are bulky due to the difference in their fibre content.

cards.title: 1.3 Routine management practices
body: Hides and manure used for fertilizer or fuel are also produced from cattle as by-products.
Cattle are divided into two groups, depending on the presence or absence of humps.
The humpless cattle adapted to temperate climatic conditions are called **Bos taurus**.
Bos taurus cattle are larger in size and therefore consume more feed than other breeds.
Zebus, however, have a greater ability to survive in warmer temperatures and are more resistant to diseases.

cards.title: Routine management practices
body: **Routine management:** identification, castration / culling, vaccination and deworming, milking hygiene, housing that is dry and ventilated, mating at the right weight (book example: a 25–30 kg doe, breed around 19–23 kg). Extensive cattle grow slowly; better feeding shortens time to market.

cards.title: 1.4 Animal housing and equipment
body: Housing also makes it easier to detect a number of disease symptoms such as diarrhoea, and to check and apply medication for external parasites such as ticks.
The owner can choose whatever fits him or her for a particular situation.
The structure has to be a place where animals can live, eat and rest comfortably.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which hormone is responsible for milk let-down in dairy cows, stimulated by washing the udder with warm water?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Washing the udder with warm water sends sensory nerve impulses to the brain, triggering the pituitary gland to release oxytocin into the bloodstream. This hormone causes contraction of the alveoli, forcing milk down into the teats.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the milk let-down hormone is **Oxytocin**.

**Conclusion**

cards.title: Animal health
body: **Health:** prevent more than cure — quarantine new animals, vaccinate, control ticks and flukes, bury or burn carcasses, keep houses clean. Common groups: bacterial, viral, parasitic (ticks, worms, flukes).

cards.title: 1.5.1 Common Diseases and Parasites Affecting Livestock
body: Causes of diseases can be infectious and non-infectious.
Causes of infectious diseases can be bacterial, viral, fungal and parasitic (internal and external parasites).
The disease is caused by a bacterium known as Mycobacterium bovis (M.bovis).
The main source of infection is the diseased animal itself.

cards.title: 1.5.2 Prevention and Control Measures for Common Diseases and Parasites
body: Prevention of diseases is much more effective and cheaper than cure.
Appropriate preventive programmes have to be designed and implemented.
For animals to be healthy, they have to be well nourished, and provided with adequate water.

questions.q: A group of students in Keren is asked to classify the farm animals of Eritrea by the structure of their feet. Into which of the following Orders is a goat correctly placed?
why: **Recall the basis of the order-level division.** The unit states that mammals are divided into orders according to the structure of their feet.
**Identify the foot structure of a goat.** A goat has an even number of functional toes or hooves.
**Match the foot structure to the correct Order.** Animals with an even number of functional toes or hooves, such as cattle, sheep, goats, camels and pigs, belong to the Order Artiodactyla.

**Test each distractor.** Perissodactyla (odd number of toes: horses and donkeys) is wrong for a goat; Aves is the Class of birds, not a mammalian order; Equidae is the Family of the horse, not the order of a goat. Only Artiodactyla is correct.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: Using the same foot-structure rule, a donkey kept for transport in Massawa must be placed in which Order?
why: **Recall the classifying criterion.** Orders of mammals in this unit are separated by the structure of the feet.
**Count the functional toes.** A donkey has an odd number of toes, so it is an odd-toed animal.
**Select the order.** Animals with an odd number of toes, such as horses and donkeys, belong to the Order Perissodactyla.

**Justify the distractors.** Artiodactyla covers even-toed animals (cattle, sheep, goats, camels, pigs); Equidae and Mammalia are the family of the horse and the class of all these mammals, not the order. The answer is B.

Of the four compartments of a ruminant stomach, the ______________ is called the true stomach because it secretes digestive juices and acids just like a human stomach.
why: **List the four compartments in order.** The four compartments of the ruminant stomach are the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum (remembered as R-R-O-A).
**Separate fore-stomachs from the glandular stomach.** The unit explains that the first three compartments are the fore-stomachs and serve as fermentation chambers.
**Identify the compartment that secretes acid.** The abomasum is the only compartment that secretes digestive juices and acids, so it is the true stomach.
**Conclude.** The blank must be filled with 'abomasum'.

questions.q:
Complete the blank in the statement below.

A newborn calf behaves like a monogastric animal because milk bypasses the rumen and passes directly to the ______________ for digestion.
why: **State the newborn calf's condition.** A newborn calf has a very small, undeveloped rumen, so for the first weeks of life it behaves like a monogastric animal.
**Trace the path of milk.** Milk bypasses the undeveloped rumen and passes directly to the single glandular compartment of the stomach.
**Name the compartment.** That compartment is the abomasum, the true stomach where acid digestion occurs.

questions.q: During a practical lesson at an agricultural school near Asmara, students dissect the stomach of a mature cow and find that the abomasum (the true stomach) has a mass of $$154\text{ g}$$. The unit table gives the composition of the mature ruminant stomach as: rumen $$80\%$$, reticulum $$5\%$$, omasum $$7-8\%$$ and abomasum $$7-8\%$$. Taking the abomasum as $$7\%$$ of the total stomach, calculate the mass of the rumen.
why: **Identify the known and the unknown.** Known: mass of abomasum $$= 154\text{ g}$$, which is $$7\%$$ of the total stomach. Unknown: mass of the rumen, which is $$80\%$$ of the total stomach.
**State the percentage principle.** Part $$= \dfrac{\text{percentage}}{100} \times \text{whole}$$, so the mass of any compartment is its percentage share of the total stomach mass.
**Find the mass of the whole stomach.** Since $$7\%$$ of the total $$= 154\text{ g}$$, the total stomach mass $$= \dfrac{154 \times 100}{7} = 2200\text{ g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of the rumen.** Mass of rumen $$= \dfrac{80}{100} \times 2200\text{ g} = 1760\text{ g}$$.

**Check the answer for reasonableness.** The rumen ($$1760\text{ g}$$) is much larger than the abomasum ($$154\text{ g}$$), which agrees with $$80\%$$ being far greater than $$7\%$$. The rumen mass is $$1760\text{ g}$$ ($$1.76\text{ kg}$$).
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A student at a livestock training centre in Keren works out that the abomasum of a mature goat makes up $$8\%$$ of the total stomach and has a mass of $$120\text{ g}$$. Using the unit's mature-animal figures (rumen $$80\%$$, reticulum $$5\%$$), find the mass of the rumen.
why: **Set out the percentages.** Abomasum $$= 8\%$$ of the total stomach and has a mass of $$120\text{ g}$$; rumen $$= 80\%$$ of the total stomach.
**Apply the percentage principle.** Part $$= \dfrac{\text{percentage}}{100} \times \text{whole}$$, therefore whole $$= \dfrac{\text{part} \times 100}{\text{percentage}}$$.
**Compute the total stomach mass.** Total $$= \dfrac{120 \times 100}{8} = 1500\text{ g}$$.
**Compute the rumen mass.** Mass of rumen $$= \dfrac{80}{100} \times 1500\text{ g} = 1200\text{ g} = 1.2\text{ kg}$$.
**State the result.** The rumen of the goat has a mass of $$1200\text{ g}$$ ($$1.2\text{ kg}$$), which is ten times the abomasum as expected from $$80\%$$ against $$8\%$$.

questions.q: A dairy farm assistant at a milk collection centre in Asmara records the reticulum of a mature cow as $$75\text{ g}$$. In the mature animal the reticulum forms $$5\%$$ and the abomasum $$7\%$$ of the total stomach. Calculate the mass of the abomasum of the same cow.
why: **Identify the known and the unknown.** Known: reticulum $$= 75\text{ g} = 5\%$$ of the total stomach. Unknown: abomasum, which is $$7\%$$ of the total stomach.
**State the percentage principle.** Because each compartment's mass comes from the same total stomach, the masses are in the same ratio as the percentages.
**Find the total stomach mass.** Total $$= \dfrac{75 \times 100}{5} = 1500\text{ g}$$.
**Calculate the abomasum mass.** Mass of abomasum $$= \dfrac{7}{100} \times 1500\text{ g} = 105\text{ g}$$.
**Check and conclude.** Since $$7\% > 5\%$$, the abomasum ($$105\text{ g}$$) is heavier than the reticulum ($$75\text{ g}$$), which is consistent. The abomasum has a mass of $$105\text{ g}$$.

questions.q: A development agent in the hot, arid lowlands of the Northern Red Sea zone advises a livestock owner to keep humped Zebu cattle rather than imported temperate cattle, while expressing a preference for exotic dairy breeds only in the cool highlands near Asmara. Using the unit's account of the two cattle species and of indigenous versus exotic breeds, explain the biological and management reasons behind this advice.
questions.answer: Zebu cattle (Bos indicus) are humped, heat-tolerant and highly resistant to tropical diseases, so they suit the hot, arid lowlands, where they match the indigenous breeds already kept in Eritrea; temperate Bos taurus and exotic dairy breeds such as Holstein-Friesian have been introduced only to raise production in specific areas such as the cool Asmara highlands, because feed, housing and healthcare must be customized to each animal's biological needs.
why: **State the two cattle species and their characteristics.** The unit explains that cattle are divided into two main species: Bos taurus, which is humpless and adapted to cool, temperate climates, and Bos indicus, the humped Zebu cattle, which are highly resistant to heat and tropical diseases.

**Link the species characters to the lowland environment.** The hot, arid lowlands impose high temperatures and a heavy burden of tropical disease, so the Zebu's heat tolerance and disease resistance make it the better biological match than the heat-sensitive, disease-susceptible Bos taurus.

**Bring in the indigenous breeds of Eritrea.** The unit states that most of Eritrea's livestock are indigenous (local) breeds, which means they are already established and suited to the local feed, climate and disease conditions of the country.

**Explain the role of exotic breeds.** Exotic breeds such as Holstein-Friesian dairy cattle have been introduced in specific areas to increase production, so they are useful where management and climate allow higher output rather than survival alone.

**Justify the highland recommendation.** The cool highlands around Asmara resemble the temperate conditions to which Bos taurus and Holstein-Friesian cattle are adapted, so the exotic dairy breed can express its production potential there with less heat and disease stress.

**Conclude with a management principle.** The unit notes that animal feed, housing and healthcare must be customized to the biological needs of each class and order, so breed choice must follow the environment and the intended purpose: hardy Zebu for survival and work in the lowlands, and exotic dairy stock for high production where conditions are favourable.

questions.q: A farmer in the lowlands of Eritrea can keep only animals that tolerate heat and resist tropical disease, while a neighbour in the cool highlands wants the highest possible milk yield. Using the unit's distinction between indigenous and exotic breeds, explain what each farmer should keep and why.
questions.answer: The lowland farmer should keep indigenous cattle such as the humped Zebu (Bos indicus), which are resistant to heat and tropical diseases and already adapted to local conditions, while the highland farmer may keep an exotic dairy breed such as the Holstein-Friesian, which has been introduced specifically to increase production and performs best where the climate is cool.
why: **Recall the indigenous-breed advantage.** Most livestock in Eritrea are indigenous (local) breeds, adapted to the country's climate, feed and disease challenge.
**Identify the lowland animal.** For heat and tropical disease, the unit points to Bos indicus (Zebu), the humped cattle that are highly resistant to heat and tropical diseases.
**Recall the exotic-breed purpose.** Exotic breeds such as the Holstein-Friesian dairy cow have been introduced in specific areas of Eritrea to increase production.

**Match breed to environment and purpose.** The lowland farmer needs survival and adaptability, so indigenous Zebu is appropriate; the highland farmer has temperate-like conditions and a production objective, so the exotic dairy breed is appropriate.
**Conclude with the general rule.** Feed, housing and healthcare must be customized to the biological needs of the animal, so breed choice must match both the environment and the production goal.

questions.q: A cooperative near Massawa wants to introduce Holstein-Friesian cows alongside its local Zebu herd, and also plans to keep poultry. Explain, using the unit's ideas of adaptation and of exotic breeds, the risks of the plan and the single management measure the unit recommends for newly purchased animals.
questions.answer: The Holstein-Friesian is an exotic dairy breed adapted to cooler conditions, so in the hot lowlands near Massawa it is exposed to heat and tropical disease stress that the local Zebu resists; the unit's recommended safeguard for newly purchased animals is quarantine, the temporary isolation of the new animals for usually $$14\text{ to }30\text{ days}$$ to ensure they are not carrying hidden infections before they join the herd.
why: **Recall the nature of the exotic breed.** The Holstein-Friesian is described as an exotic dairy breed introduced in specific areas to increase production, not as a heat- and disease-resistant local breed.
**Compare with the local Zebu.** Bos indicus (Zebu) cattle are highly resistant to heat and tropical diseases, whereas Bos taurus cattle are adapted to cool, temperate climates.

**Deduce the risk near Massawa.** In the hot lowlands the imported Holstein-Friesian would face heat and tropical disease stress that the resident Zebu tolerates, so production and survival may be poor.
**Recall the safeguard for new stock.** The unit states that quarantine is the temporary isolation of newly purchased animals for usually $$14\text{ to }30\text{ days}$$ to detect hidden infections.

**State the recommendation.** The cooperative should quarantine the newly purchased cattle for $$14\text{ to }30\text{ days}$$ before mixing them with the local herd, and should expect that the exotic breed needs housing, feed and healthcare customized to its biological needs.

units.title: Forestry and Wildlife
units.intro: Forests and wild animals are one system: trees give habitat, food and cover; wildlife spreads seed. Eritrea once had more closed highland forest (juniper, olive). Much is now woodland, bush or scrub after cutting, burning and overgrazing.

cards.title: 2.1.1 Interrelationships between Forests and Wildlife
body: The interrelationship between forests and wild animals is manifested in a life structure.
The interaction of a community with the non-living environment constitutes an ecosystem.
Every wild animal has a specific habitat in a forest.
Forests provide shelter to wild animals and supply them with all the necessary materials for their survival and development.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Historical Background and Existing Status
body: In Eritrea, forest covers about 1 % of the land area.
With the destruction of forests, wildlife lose their habitats and this leads to their extinction.
Closed to open forest cover still exists in the Semenawi-Bahri and riverine areas.
The mangrove which is marine (littoral) forest is found in the northern and southern Red Sea areas of Eritrea.

cards.title: Forests
body: **Classes:** closed forest vs woodland vs plantation vs mangrove on the coast. Conservation: enclosures, enrichment planting, energy-saving stoves, alternative energy, wildlife law and protected areas (wild ass, ibex, remaining elephant range in Gash-Barka).

cards.title: 2.2.1 Classification of Forests
body: Forests are classified based on age, species composition, mode of regeneration, uses or management objectives, growing stock, exploitation, biotic interference, ecology and canopy condition.
Based on age, forests may be even aged (regular) – or uneven aged (irregular) or selection forest.
Likewise, based on species composition, forests can be pure (mainly composed of one species) or mixed (composed of two or more species) intermingled in the same canopy.
Pure plantation forests are called **monoculture**.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Classification of Forests in Eritrea
body: Based on their geographical distribution, forests of Eritrea are classified into four major groups.

Highland forests Highland forests are mainly dry montane forest composed of a mixture of coniferous tree species such as Juniperus procera and broad-leaved species such as Olea africana and their associated species.
Forests at low and medium altitude The forests at low and medium altitudes are essentially composed of dry deciduous forests and tickets.
Mixed woodlands are composed of acacia and associated tree species.

cards.title: 2.2.3 The Role of forests
body: Forests have intangible and tangible roles.
Effective sound barriers: Trees soften urban noise.
Trees, planted in a neighbourhood or around houses muffle noise from freeways and airports.
Trees produce oxygen: In one season, a mature leafy tree produces as much oxygen as 10 people inhale in a year.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Deforestation
body: **Deforestation** is a human-induced process in which an existing forest cover is removed for various reasons.
Natural factors that cause deforestation include volcanic eruptions and hurricanes.
With the introduction of commercial farming, forests gave way to large-scale mechanised agriculture.
Increasing population pressure extended land clearing to steep areas, which were previously unsuitable for cultivation.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Afforestation and Reforestation
body: **Afforestation** is the planting seeds or tree seedlings to create a forest on land which has not recently been forest for example where there had not any trees for the last 20 years, or in an area, which has never been a forest.
Reforestation, on the other hand, is the re-establishment of a forest after the removal of trees for timber.
Eritrea has experienced centuries of deforestation and is now engaged in reforestation programmes to restore these lost forests.
Tree planting initiatives can be undertaken almost anywhere.

cards.title: 2.2.6 Seedling Planting
body: **A nursery** is an area where plant materials are produced under controlled conditions in order to produce strong, healthy, hardy seedlings for planting.
The majority of species planted in reforestation, in Eritrea, are grown from seeds as not many of them are amenable to vegetative propagation.
Seedlings can be raised in containers such as pots or tubes or as bare-root seedlings grown directly at the nursery site or in the field.
Experiences show that, in semi arid conditions, where the amount of rainfall is low and unreliable, survival is improved if containerized seedlings are used for planting.

cards.title: 2.2.7 Time for Planting
body: Planting is carried out soon after the onset of the rainy season, when rain can be confidentially expected during planting or afterwards.
Before transporting to the planting sites, the seedlings should be thoroughly watered.
If seedlings are stored before planting, they should be protected from excessive heat and direct sunlight.
Seedlings raised on black polythene bags can be easily damaged if exposed to the sun.

cards.title: 2.2.8 Enclosures/Closure
body: **Enclosure or closure** means an area that has been put under full or partial protection by restricting human-induced activities such as livestock grazing.
Enclosures are usually located on steep slopes.
Restriction is put in place for a number of years until regrowth of the natural vegetation has occurred.
Enclosures for the rehabilitation of degraded lands have now been widely established throughout Eritrea.

cards.title: 2.2.9 Regeneration Methods
body: Forests may regenerate from seeds, coppice or plantations from seedlings raised in nurseries.
**Regeneration** is the replacement of old individual plants by younger members of the same species.
**Regeneration** refers to the normal growth and development of individual plants from seedlings, to saplings and finally to an adult tree.
Certain processes affect the transition from one life stage to next.

cards.title: 2.2.10 Parkland Agroforestry
body: **Agroforestry** is an integrated approach to forestry which uses the interactive benefits obtained by combining trees and shrubs with crops and/or livestock.
Integration can be achieved either in a spatial mixture or in a temporal sequence.

Agroforestry systems offer increased productivity, greater economic benefits, positive social outcomes and provide a wider spectrum of ecological goods and services, when compared with conventional agricultural and forest production methods.
Agroforestry has the potential to help reduce climate change since trees take up and store carbon at a faster rate than crop plants.

cards.title: 2.3.1 The Role of Wildlife
body: Stone Age people and hunter-gatherers relied on plant and wildlife for their food.
Early human hunters may have hunted some species to extinction.
Today, hunting, fishing or gathering wildlife is still a significant food source in many parts of the world.
In others, hunting and recreational fishing are sport or recreation and the edible meat is seen as a side benefit.

cards.title: 2.3.2 The Classification of Wildlife
body: Based on their habitat, wildlife can be classified as: • aquatic (freshwater and marine wildlife) • terrestrial wildlife (forest, desert, savannah and mountain wildlife).

cards.title: 2.3.3 Causes of Wildlife Decline
body: Globally, the causes for wildlife decline are diverse, depending on the local environmental and socio-economic conditions.
Habitat destruction and fragmentation The habitat of a given species is its preferred area or territory.
Human settlements decrease the carrying capacity of wildlife.
Consequently, wildlife populations remain confined to islands, littoral or habitat which is in effect island-like for the species concerned.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Human and Wildlife Conflict and Conflict Resolution

The general framework for organising information about state of the environment – driving forces-pressures-state-impactsresponses (DPSIR) – is used to analyse the problem.
DPSIR looks into causes, effects and possible solutions to the underlying problems.
Driving forces refer to the human activities and socio-economic developments causing the problem.

cards.q: What is the primary ecological disadvantage of bare-root seedlings compared to containerized seedlings?

options.A: They are too heavy to transport.
options.B: They are highly susceptible to root drying (desiccation).

options.E: They take a longer time to mature in the nursery.

cards.title: 2.4.1 Community Forestry
body: The term “community forestry” is applied in many different ways.
Through their involvement in community forestry, the inhabitants recognize and take advantage of the economic, social and environmental opportunities afforded by their local forest resources.
Participation of the local people is essential in all aspects, including the conservation and sustainable use of natural resources.
The focus, however, of community forest management is on the participation of the local communities in order that they may manage their forests themselves.

cards.title: 2.4.2 Law Enforcement
body: Since then, tree planting on hillsides (afforestation and reforestation), agroforestry and soil and water conservation measures have been implemented.

questions.q: In a highland forest near Segeneyti, tall canopy trees intercept most of the incoming sunlight, so that small herb species growing on the forest floor receive too little light to grow well. The canopy trees themselves are not affected by the herbs in any way. Which type of species interaction does this describe?

options.A: Commensalism, because one species benefits and the other is unaffected.
options.B: Amensalism, because one species is harmed while the other is unaffected.
options.C: Mutualism, because both species benefit from the interaction.
options.D: Competition, because both species are negatively affected.

why: **Identify the effect on each species.** Record the sign of the effect on both partners. The small forest herbs are harmed (they receive too little light, so they grow poorly), while the tall canopy trees are unaffected by the herbs' presence.

**Write the interaction as signs.** Harmed species = negative ($$ - $$); unaffected species = neutral ($$ 0 $$). The interaction is therefore ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$) when read from the canopy tree to the herb.

**Match the sign pattern to the interaction type.** From the unit's interaction table, ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$) is amensalism, exactly matching the unit example of large trees blocking light from reaching small forest herbs. Commensalism is ($$ + $$, $$ 0 $$), mutualism is ($$ + $$, $$ + $$) and competition is ($$ - $$, $$ - $$), so none of the other options fits the observed signs.

**Reject the strongest distractor.** Option A is the classic misconception: it corrects the sign pattern of commensalism. In commensalism one species benefits (for example orchids gaining light by growing on high forest tree branches); here the herbs gain nothing at all, so commensalism cannot be correct.

questions.q: Along a riverbank in the Gash-Barka lowlands, orchids grow on the high branches of a large tree, where they receive the light they need; the tree is neither helped nor harmed by the orchids. Which type of species interaction is this?
questions.answer: Commensalism (+/0): one species (the orchid) benefits and the other (the tree) is unaffected.
why: **State the effect on each species.** The orchids benefit because they gain a raised, well-lit growing position on the tree's branches; the tree is unaffected because the orchids neither help nor harm it.

**Assign signs and match the unit pattern.** Effect signs are ($$ + $$, $$ 0 $$), which the unit's table lists as commensalism, using the very example of orchids growing on high forest tree branches for light.

**Distinguish from mutualism and antagonism.** If the tree also benefited, the interaction would be mutualism ($$ + $$, $$ + $$); if the tree were harmed, it would be antagonism ($$ + $$, $$ - $$). Since the tree is unaffected, only commensalism fits.

questions.q: A woodland herb is heavily shaded by a large overstorey tree and therefore grows poorly, while the tree's growth is unaffected. A student writes that this is competition between the tree and the herb. Is the student correct? Justify your answer using the unit's interaction types.
questions.answer: No. Competition requires both species to be negatively affected ($$ - $$, $$ - $$), but here the tree is unaffected, so the interaction is amensalism ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$).
why: **State the definition of competition.** In competition both species are negatively affected because they compete for the same limited resource, such as light, water or soil nutrients.

**Test the observed situation against that definition.** The herb is harmed (negative), but the large tree is unaffected (neutral), because the herb takes no resource the tree needs in limiting supply.

**Conclude and correct the classification.** Since the effect pair is ($$ 0 $$, $$ - $$) and not ($$ - $$, $$ - $$), competition is ruled out; the correct label is amensalism (one species harmed, the other unaffected).

questions.q: A reforestation project in the Central Highlands near Asmara will plant tree seedlings on a degraded site measuring $$15\text{ hectares}$$ at the standard recommended spacing of $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$. Calculate the number of tree seedlings required.
why: **Identify the given data and what is asked.** Given: total planting area = $$15\text{ hectares}$$; spacing = $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$. Required: the total number of seedlings. The unit gives the standard density that accompanies this spacing.

**State the density principle.** The standard recommended spacing of $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ corresponds to a planting density of $$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$, because each seedling occupies a $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ square.
**Set up the multiplication.** Total seedlings = density $$\times$$ area = $$2\,500\text{ seedlings/ha} \times 15\text{ ha}$$.
**Carry out the arithmetic.** $$2\,500 \times 15 = 37\,500$$ seedlings.

**State the result with units.** The project requires $$37\,500\text{ tree seedlings}$$ at $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing. A sensible follow-up for the project manager is to add a few percent extra seedlings to replace any that die after planting.

questions.q: Historical records show that forest cover in Eritrea was approximately $$30\%$$ of the total land area in 1912, and that this had fallen to $$11\%$$ by 1952. Calculate the average annual decrease in forest cover over that period, in percentage points per year. Then convert this annual loss into square kilometres per year, taking Eritrea's total land area as $$125\,000\text{ km}^2$$.
questions.answer: The average annual decrease was $$0.475\text{ percentage points per year}$$, equivalent to approximately $$593.75\text{ km}^2\text{ (about }594\text{ km}^2\text{) of forest lost per year}$$.
why: **Extract the data from the record.** Forest cover in 1912 = $$30\%$$; forest cover in 1952 = $$11\%$$. Time elapsed = $$1952 - 1912 = 40\text{ years}$$.
**Find the total decline in percentage points.** Decline = $$30\% - 11\% = 19\text{ percentage points}$$.
**Divide by the number of years.** Average annual decrease = $$\dfrac{19\text{ percentage points}}{40\text{ years}} = 0.475\text{ percentage points per year}$$.
**Convert one percentage point into an area.** $$1\%$$ of $$125\,000\text{ km}^2 = \dfrac{125\,000}{100} = 1\,250\text{ km}^2$$.
**Convert the annual rate into square kilometres.** Area lost per year = $$0.475 \times 1\,250\text{ km}^2 = 593.75\text{ km}^2\text{ per year}$$ (approximately $$594\text{ km}^2\text{ per year}$$).

**Interpret the result.** Forest was being lost at an average rate of about $$0.475$$ percentage points per year, roughly $$594\text{ km}^2$$ of forest per year, between 1912 and 1952. The unit attributes such decline to land clearing for agriculture, overgrazing, timber extraction, firewood collection, recurrent droughts and the destructive effects of war.

**Multiply by the total land area.** Remaining forest = $$0.11 \times 125\,000\text{ km}^2 = 13\,750\text{ km}^2$$.
**Conclude.** Only $$13\,750\text{ km}^2$$ was still under forest in 1952, which shows how far the $$30\%$$ cover of 1912 had already been eroded.

questions.q: A forest block of $$10\text{ hectares}$$ in the Semenawi-Bahri highlands is surveyed and found to have a tree canopy covering $$15\,000\text{ m}^2$$. Using the unit's classification by canopy density, how should this forest be classified?

options.A: As an open forest, because its canopy coverage is at least $$10\%$$ with a discontinuous canopy.
options.B: As a closed forest, because its canopy coverage exceeds $$20\%$$.
options.C: As a primary forest, because the canopy is undisturbed by human activity.
options.D: As an uneven-aged forest, because canopy cover varies from place to place.

why: **Convert the forest area to square metres.** $$1\text{ hectare} = 10\,000\text{ m}^2$$, so the block covers $$10 \times 10\,000 = 100\,000\text{ m}^2$$.
**Find the percentage canopy coverage.** Canopy coverage $$= \dfrac{15\,000\text{ m}^2}{100\,000\text{ m}^2} \times 100\% = 15\%$$.

**Apply the canopy-density definitions.** A closed forest has canopy coverage greater than $$20\%$$; an open forest has discontinuous canopy coverage of at least $$10\%$$ with a continuous grass layer underneath. Since $$15\%$$ is below $$20\%$$ but above $$10\%$$, the block is an open forest.

**Check the distractors one by one.** B is wrong because $$15\%$$ does not exceed $$20\%$$. C is wrong because primary forest is a classification by level of human interference, not by canopy density. D is wrong because even-aged or uneven-aged is a classification by age, and canopy variation is not the stated criterion. Only A states a criterion and conclusion consistent with the unit, so it is the unique correct option.

questions.q: A 40-hectare dry montane forest near Nakfa has a tree canopy covering $$96\,000\text{ m}^2$$. Classify this forest by canopy density using the unit's definitions.

why: **Convert hectares to square metres.** $$40\text{ hectares} = 40 \times 10\,000 = 400\,000\text{ m}^2$$.
**Calculate the canopy percentage.** Coverage $$= \dfrac{96\,000}{400\,000} \times 100\% = 24\%$$.
**Compare with the threshold.** A closed forest has canopy coverage greater than $$20\%$$. Since $$24\% > 20\%$$, the forest is closed.

questions.q: According to the unit, a forest whose canopy coverage is greater than $$20\%$$ is classified as a ______ forest, while a forest with discontinuous canopy coverage of at least $$10\%$$ and a continuous grass layer underneath is classified as an ______ forest.
questions.answer: A closed forest (greater than $$20\%$$ canopy coverage) and an open forest (discontinuous canopy of at least $$10\%$$ with a continuous grass layer underneath).
why: **Recall the canopy-density classes.** The unit classifies forests by canopy density into closed forest and open forest, using canopy coverage as the distinguishing measure.

**Match each definition to its term.** Greater than $$20\%$$ canopy coverage defines a closed forest; discontinuous canopy coverage of at least $$10\%$$ with a continuous grass layer underneath defines an open forest.

**State the completed sentence.** The sentence reads: greater than $$20\%$$ canopy coverage gives a closed forest, while $$10\%$$ or more with a discontinuous canopy and a continuous grass layer gives an open forest.

questions.q: A restoration team is given a fixed supply of $$5\,000$$ tree seedlings for a dry site on the Buri Peninsula. The unit states that the standard spacing of $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ gives a density of $$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$, and that in drier areas the spacing is increased to $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ to reduce competition for water. (a) Calculate the number of seedlings per hectare at the wider $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing. (b) Determine how many hectares the $$5\,000$$ seedlings can plant at this dry-site spacing, and state how much more area this covers than the same $$5\,000$$ seedlings would cover at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing.
questions.answer: (a) $$1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$ (exactly $$\frac{10\,000}{9}$$) at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing. (b) The $$5\,000$$ seedlings can plant $$4.5\text{ hectares}$$ at the dry-site spacing, which is $$2.5\text{ hectares}$$ more than the $$2\text{ hectares}$$ they would plant at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing.
why: **Establish the area occupied by one seedling.** At $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing each seedling occupies a square of side $$3\text{ m}$$, so each seedling occupies $$3 \times 3 = 9\text{ m}^2$$.
**Convert one hectare to square metres.** $$1\text{ hectare} = 10\,000\text{ m}^2$$, the unit conversion needed to express the density per hectare.

**Calculate the density at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$.** (a) Density $$= \dfrac{10\,000\text{ m}^2\text{ per hectare}}{9\text{ m}^2\text{ per seedling}} = 1\,111.1\ldots \approx 1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$.

**Cross-check the density with the standard spacing.** For comparison, the unit's standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing gives $$\dfrac{10\,000}{4} = 2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$, which matches the unit value and confirms the method. Widening the spacing from $$2\text{ m}$$ to $$3\text{ m}$$ therefore more than halves the number of seedlings needed per hectare.

**Find the area plantable at the dry-site spacing.** (b) Area $$= \dfrac{\text{number of seedlings}}{\text{density}} = \dfrac{5\,000\text{ seedlings}}{1\,111.1\text{ seedlings per hectare}} = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$. Equivalently, $$5\,000 \times 9\text{ m}^2 = 45\,000\text{ m}^2 = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$.
**Find the area the same supply would cover at standard spacing.** At $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, area $$= \dfrac{5\,000}{2\,500} = 2\text{ hectares}$$.

**Compare the two areas and conclude.** The extra area covered $$= 4.5 - 2 = 2.5\text{ hectares}$$. So $$5\,000$$ seedlings plant $$4.5$$ hectares at the dry-site spacing of $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$, which is $$2.5$$ hectares more than the same supply would plant at the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ spacing. This is why the unit recommends wider spacing in drier areas: each seedling has more soil water available and competition for water is reduced.

questions.q: A nursery allocates $$9\,000$$ seedlings to a dry lowland enclosure site along the Anseba where foresters decide to use the wider $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ spacing ($$1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$) instead of the standard $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$ ($$2\,500\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$). (a) How many hectares can be planted at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$? (b) How many hectares would the same $$9\,000$$ seedlings have covered at $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, and what is the difference?
questions.answer: (a) $$8.1\text{ hectares}$$ at $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$. (b) $$3.6\text{ hectares}$$ at $$2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$$, a difference of $$4.5\text{ hectares}$$.
why: **Use the dry-site density.** At $$3\text{ m} \times 3\text{ m}$$ each seedling occupies $$9\text{ m}^2$$, giving $$\dfrac{10\,000}{9} \approx 1\,111\text{ seedlings per hectare}$$.
**Calculate the area at the wider spacing.** (a) Area $$= \dfrac{9\,000}{1\,111.1} = 8.1\text{ hectares}$$; equivalently $$9\,000 \times 9 = 81\,000\text{ m}^2 = 8.1\text{ hectares}$$.
**Calculate the area at the standard spacing.** (b) Area $$= \dfrac{9\,000}{2\,500} = 3.6\text{ hectares}$$.
**Compare and conclude.** Difference $$= 8.1 - 3.6 = 4.5\text{ hectares}$$, so the wider spacing allows the same nursery supply to cover $$4.5$$ hectares more land.

questions.q: In a Parkland Agroforestry system, multipurpose trees such as Balanites aegyptiaca and Faidherbia albida are kept at widely spaced intervals of $$10\text{ to }20\text{ trees per hectare}$$ among annual crops. (a) What average area, in square metres, is available to each tree if $$10\text{ trees}$$ are kept per hectare? (b) State one reason given in the unit for keeping the trees so widely spaced.
questions.answer: (a) $$1\,000\text{ m}^2$$ of land per tree at $$10\text{ trees per hectare}$$. (b) Wide spacing lets the trees provide livestock feed, fuel wood and shade without blocking too much sunlight from the crops growing below.
why: **Convert the hectare to square metres.** $$1\text{ hectare} = 10\,000\text{ m}^2$$.
**Divide the area by the number of trees.** (a) Area per tree $$= \dfrac{10\,000\text{ m}^2}{10\text{ trees}} = 1\,000\text{ m}^2\text{ per tree}$$.

Faidherbia albida helps further through reverse phenology: it sheds leaves in the wet season and keeps them in the dry season.

cards.title: 3.1.1 Definition of Soil and Water Conservation
body: Soil and water conservation refers to practices which involve all human activities aimed at reducing the removal of the soil from the land, as well as protecting and maintaining the water supply.

cards.title: 3.1.2 The Importance of Soil and Water Conservation
body: Soil and water conservation has long history in Eritrea.

Farming has been carried out for thousands of years, and traditional soil and water conservation methods have evolved at the local level in response to the evolution of the agricultural system in Eritrea.
Eritrea is located in the Sudano-Sahelian region of Africa, where rainfall is not only low but also erratic, with great variations between years.
Precipitation is unevenly distributed geographically, with large parts of the country being too dry for rain-fed agriculture.

Thus, salinization is **the accumulation of excess soluble salts in the root zone**.

cards.title: 3.2.1 Types of Land Degradation
body: **Land degradation** is a process that lowers the current and/ or potential capability of land to produce goods and services.
Continued deterioration of land leads to a permanent decrease in its biological potential and deterioration of living conditions for the inhabitants.
Land degradation is both a process and a phenomenon.

As a process, land degradation is continuous and incremental, and marked by increased weakening of the physical, biological and economic potential of the land through a drastic reduction in overall productivity.

cards.title: 3.2.2 Causes and Effects of Land Degradation
body: The main causes for land degradation are complex and attributed to a combination of biophysical, social, economic and political factors.
One such view considers population pressure to be the main cause of deforestation, overgrazing and expansion of cultivation into marginal lands.
High population density is not necessarily related to land degradation; it is what a population does to the land that determines the extent of degradation.
People can be a major asset in reversing a trend towards degradation.

cards.title: 3.2.3 Soil Erosion
body: **Erosion** is a gravity driven process that transports solids in the natural environment and deposits them elsewhere.
**Erosion** is a natural process, but its magnitude has increased dramatically due to human land-use practices, especially industrial agriculture, deforestation and urban sprawl.
Land that is used for industrial agriculture generally experiences a significantly faster rate of erosion than land under natural vegetation, or land used for sustainable agricultural practices.
Tillage reduces vegetation cover on the surface of the soil and disturbs both soil structure and plant roots that would otherwise hold the soil in place.

body: Vertical interval (VI) is the difference in height (elevation) between two points on a slope.
Slope steepness can be expressed in four different ways: • Angle in degrees: This is the angle that the slope makes with the horizontal.
Metres per metre: This is vertical interval divided by horizontal.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Physical SWC Measures
body: Physical SWC measures usually comprise engineering works involving the construction of earthworks such as terraces, earth dams and water diversions.
The earthworks intercept and slow runoff water, which then prevent sheet, rill and gully erosion.
The intercepted water soaks into the soil.
Hillside terraces: A hillside terrace is hillside ditch or ridge for controlling the flow of surface water down a slope.

cards.title: 3.3.3 Biological SWC Measures
body: Vegetative SWC measures can be used in various land uses.
Vegetative conservation measures can be used on uncultivated hillsides, to conserve cultivated lands and for the protection of riverbanks.

cards.title: 3.3.4 Agronomic Practices
body: Agronomic practices are those cultural or biological practices for management of annual and perennial crops that promote SWC.
Soil management can be defined as the sum total of all tillage operations, cropping practices, fertilizer, lime and other treatments conducted on, or applied to, a soil for the production of plants.

**Water management** is the techniques and practices through which available water (rainwater, floodwater, plant available water in soils) is conserved and used with minimum wastage for sustainable agricultural production.
Soil and water management include all farming practices applied on land, through which soils and water are conserved and used with minimum wastage for sustained agricultural production.

Surface water is stored either in natural lakes and wetlands or in artificial storage structures created by the construction of dams.
Dams are constructed for the purpose of water storage for irrigation, hydro-electric power generation, flood control or any combination of these.

cards.title: 3.4.2 Ponds
body: Ponds are bodies of water created by excavating a pit or by constructing a short embankment across a water source.
Ponds are used to store small supplies of water.
In Eritrea, all ponds are small, with a capacity of 500–5000 m3 of water, and are used for short periods of time.
The number of ponds is increasing, especially in places where the climate is arid.

cards.title: Irrigation and drainage
body: Water conservation = store (ponds, dams), sink (infiltration), save (mulch, drip where possible), don’t waste or pollute.

cards.title: 3.5.1 Irrigation
body: **Irrigation** is the process by which water is conveyed from the source to the crop through open or closed canals or pipes.

Archaeological investigation has identified evidence of irrigation in Mesopotamia, Egypt and Iran which were built as far back as the 6th millennium BCE, where barley was grown in areas where the natural rainfall was insufficient to support such a crop.
In many parts of the world, there is a deficiency of soil water for crop production for part or all the year, and staple crop production depends on irrigation.
The use of ground water for irrigation enables the extension of the irrigated area.

cards.title: 3.5.2 The Importance of Irrigation
body: Agriculture is often cited as the principal “user” of raw water.
In arid and semi-arid areas, irrigation is used to extend cultivation, to increase yield and to insure against high rainfall variability.
In humid areas, supplementary irrigation is used to overcome the soil water deficit that may occur at a critical period of the cropgrowing season.
Water infiltrates into the soil, evaporates or runs off as surface water.

cards.title: 3.5.3 Methods of Irrigation
body: Various types of irrigation technique differ on how the water obtained from the source is distributed within the field.
In general, the object of irrigation is to supply the entire field uniformly with water so that each plant has the amount of water it needs – neither too much nor too little.
Surface irrigation is usually relatively cheaper to install but more expensive to operate.
Modern irrigation systems are relatively expensive, and offer lower operating costs and higher water-use efficiency.

cards.title: 3.5.4 Drainage
body: **Drainage** is a practice of removing excess water from the soil surface and upper layer of the sub-soil, in order to improve the soil conditions for growing crops.
Poorly drained soils are not well aerated due to saturation with water.
Soil fertility in poorly drained soils is very low, giving rise to patchy plants with stunted roots and reduced growth.

cards.title: 3.5.5 The Importance of Drainage
body: In moist climates, soils may be adequate for cropping, with the exception of when they become waterlogged for brief periods each year from snow melt or heavy rains.
Soils that are predominantly clay filter water very slowly downward, meanwhile, plant roots suffocate because the excessive water around the roots eliminates aeration in the soil.
Other soils may have an impervious layer of mineralized soil, called a hardpan, or a relatively impervious rock layer may underlie shallow soils.
Excellent soils may be waterlogged for one week of the year, which is sufficient enough to kill fruit trees, causing a loss of land productivity until replacements can be established.

cards.title: 3.5.6 Types of Drainage Systems
body: Shallow ditches, also called open drains, normally accomplish surface drainage.
The shallow ditches discharge into larger and deeper collection drains.
In order to facilitate the flow of excess water toward the drains, the field is given an artificial slope by means of land grading.
When compared to surface and sub-surface drainage systems, this method works well in poorly permeable topsoil overlying rapidly permeable and deep sub-soil.

options.A: It prevents the leaves from absorbing too much nitrogen.
options.B: Fruit tree roots suffocate and can die if waterlogged for even a week.

Biological: Cover crops, grass strips, afforestation, enclosures, controlled grazing.
Mechanical: Contour ploughing, terraces and bunds, check dams, cut-off drains, sub-surface dams in sandy wadis.

questions.q: While inspecting a gently sloping cropland near Keren, a farmer finds many small, shallow, parallel channels running down the field, each only about 20 cm deep. Which type of water erosion is this, and why can the farmer still correct it with ordinary tillage?

options.A: Splash erosion, because raindrop impact has formed a hard surface crust
options.B: Sheet erosion, because the channels are broad, thin sheets of flowing water
options.C: Rill erosion, because these are small, shallow, concentrated flow channels that ordinary farm tillage can smooth out
options.D: Gully erosion, because the channels are narrow and deep and cannot be destroyed by normal tillage

why: **Recall the classification of water erosion.** The unit divides water erosion into four types: splash (raindrop) erosion, sheet erosion, rill erosion and gully erosion.

**Match the field evidence to a type.** The field shows small, shallow, concentrated flow paths (channels) rather than craters from raindrop impact or a uniform thin sheet of moving water. Small, shallow, concentrated flow paths are the defining feature of rill erosion.

**Check the depth against the unit data.** The unit records rill channels as up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep, so the measured 20 cm depth falls inside the rill range, while gullies are $$1 - 150\text{ meters}$$ deep.
**Decide on correctability.** The unit states that rills are temporary and can easily be smoothed out by ordinary farm tillage operations, unlike gullies, which cannot be destroyed by normal tillage.

**Evaluate the distractors.** A is wrong because splash erosion creates small craters and a hard crust, not channels. B is wrong because sheet erosion removes soil uniformly in broad, thin sheets, not in defined small channels. D is wrong because the channels are shallow and the unit reserves the non-tillable, deep category for gullies.

**Rule out the other types.** There is no uniform removal of soil down the slope in thin sheets (sheet), no concentrated channels (rill) and no deep, incised channel (gully).

questions.q: A forester uses a line level to check the slope of a gently sloping cropland near Keren before laying out contour bunds. The two identical sticks are set $$10\text{ meters}$$ apart, and the reading on the stick at the lower ground position is $$0.9\text{ meters}$$ greater than the reading on the stick at the higher ground position. Calculate the percentage slope of the plot and state, with justification, whether the site is suitable for contour bunds.
questions.answer: Percentage slope = $$9\%$$; this is slightly steeper than the $$2\% - 8\%$$ ideal range for contour bunds, so bund spacing must be tightened or a stronger physical measure such as hillside terracing used.
why: **Identify what the line level measures.** The unit describes the line level as two identical $$1.5\text{-meter}$$ sticks connected by a $$10\text{-meter}$$ cotton string with a small spirit level suspended in the middle. Because the string is exactly $$10\text{ meters}$$ long, the horizontal interval (HI) is the fixed stick spacing of $$10\text{ meters}$$.

**Obtain the vertical interval.** The vertical interval (VI) is the difference in elevation between the two points. Since both sticks stand vertically, the difference in reading on the sticks equals the difference in ground elevation: $$\text{VI} = 0.9\text{ meters}$$.
**Name the percentage slope formula.** The unit gives $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{\text{VI}}{\text{HI}}\right) \times 100$$.
**Substitute the measured values.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{0.9}{10}\right) \times 100 = 0.09 \times 100 = 9\%$$.

**Compare the slope with the ideal site for contour bunds.** The unit table states that contour bunds intercept surface runoff and encourage infiltration on gently sloping croplands of $$2\% - 8\%$$ slope. The computed slope of $$9\%$$ is slightly steeper than that ideal range.

**Conclude with a justified recommendation.** The plot is at $$9\%$$ slope, just above the $$2\% - 8\%$$ band for which contour bunds are the recommended physical measure. Contour bunds would need closer spacing and careful design, and on such a slope a stronger structural measure such as hillside terraces, which break slope length and trap water and sediment on sloping cultivated hills, should be considered.

**Substitute and compute.** $$\text{Percentage Slope} = \left(\dfrac{0.4}{10}\right) \times 100 = 0.04 \times 100 = 4\%$$.

questions.q: Describe the transition of water erosion from splash erosion to the formation of a highly advanced gully system on a bare, sloping farm plot in the highlands. In your answer, name each stage in order, state the characteristic feature and approximate depth or scale of each, and explain how the farmer could detect the earliest stage of uniform soil removal before channels appear.
questions.answer: The sequence is splash (raindrop) erosion (micro-scale craters, hard crust, particles splashed up to $$1.5\text{ m}$$) then sheet erosion (uniform removal in broad, thin sheets, detectable early by soil pedestals) then rill erosion (small, shallow concentrated channels up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep, removable by ordinary tillage) then gully erosion (narrow, deep channels of $$1 - 150\text{ m}$$ that fragment the land and cannot be destroyed by normal tillage).
why: **Start with detachment by raindrop impact.** The process begins with splash (raindrop) erosion, the detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by direct raindrop impact on bare soil. On a micro-scale it produces small craters, destroys soil structure and forms a hard crust on dry soil; the unit notes raindrops can strike bare soil at speeds up to $$30\text{ kilometers per hour}$$ and splash particles up to $$1.5\text{ meters}$$ horizontally.

**Move to uniform removal as sheet erosion.** Once detached, particles are removed uniformly down the slope by water flowing overland in broad, thin sheets rather than in defined channels. Sheet erosion strips very thin layers, removing the most fertile topsoil and organic matter and exposing stone bases.

**Explain how to detect the sheet stage early.** The unit pro-tip advises looking for soil pedestals - tiny columns of soil capped by small stones or wood chips that have protected the soil directly underneath from raindrop impact. Their appearance signals that the surrounding soil is being stripped away in thin sheets before any channels form.

**Describe the appearance of concentrated flow paths.** As overland flow concentrates, rill erosion develops small, shallow, concentrated flow paths that appear as many small, parallel channels across the field, up to $$30\text{ cm}$$ deep. Rills are temporary and can be easily smoothed out by ordinary tillage, so the unit pro-tip warns that if left untreated for even one rainy season they merge and deepen.

**Explain the final, advanced stage.** In the advanced stage the runoff flows in narrow, deep channels during or immediately after heavy rains, producing gullies. Gullies range from $$1\text{ to }2\text{ meters}$$ to over $$75\text{ meters}$$ deep (the unit table gives $$1 - 150\text{ meters}$$), with wide, steep, unstable walls that cannot be destroyed by normal tillage operations.

**State the consequence and the conclusion.** The gully divides the land into fragments and stops machinery movement, making reclamation extremely difficult and expensive. The correct conclusion is that the stages form a continuous, accelerating chain - splash to sheet to rill to gully - so intervention at the rill stage (or earlier, by spotting soil pedestals and applying biological or physical conservation measures) is far cheaper than reclaiming a mature gully.

questions.q: Explain how wind erosion acts on a dry, bare lowland plain such as the eastern dry lowlands, naming its two main effects and describing the damage each does to soil and crops.
questions.answer: Wind erosion acts through deflation, the lifting and removal of loose, light soil particles to another region, and abrasion, the wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended soil particles carried in high-velocity winds; together they strip topsoil and damage seedlings.
why: **State where wind erosion occurs.** The unit states that wind erosion occurs primarily in arid and semi-arid climates where the soil is dry and unprotected by vegetation, which describes the dry lowlands receiving only about $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$ of soil loss by wind.
**Define the first effect.** Deflation is the lifting and removal of loose, light soil particles to another region. It is the primary cause of topsoil blowing away from dry lowland fields.

**Define the second effect.** Abrasion is the wearing away of plants, rocks and structures by suspended soil particles carried in high-velocity winds, and the unit table records it as sand abrasion on seedlings.

**Conclude on the agricultural impact.** Because the dry lowlands have only wind - not rainfall runoff - as the primary causative agent, the conservation response must protect the surface, for example by maintaining vegetative cover and mulch rather than by constructing water-intercepting structures.

questions.q: Explain how rainfall and topography combine to make the Eritrean highlands the most erosion-prone area in the unit's comparison of regions, and state the specific consequences this has for crop production there.
questions.answer: In the highlands, high and intense rainfall produces large volumes of runoff that steep topography accelerates downslope, giving an estimated soil loss of $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, the highest of the four regions; the consequences are exposed plant roots, severe yield reduction and loss of topsoil.
why: **Recall the two controlling factors.** The unit states that the speed and extent of soil degradation depend on factors such as soil types, topography, climate and the intensity of land use - here climate (rainfall) and topography (slope) are decisive.

**Explain the role of the rainfall factor.** Rainfall in these highland areas supplies the water that detaches particles by raindrop impact and then carries them downslope as runoff, so water is listed as the primary causative agent for the highlands.

**Explain the role of the topographic factor.** Slope steepness increases the velocity of runoff, so the water has more energy to detach and transport soil. The unit records measured soil loss on steep slopes of $$3.4\text{ to }84.5\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$, with a mean of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$ - about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil annually and roughly $$20\text{ times}$$ the soil replacement rate.

**Apply the regional comparison.** In the unit's table the highlands have the highest estimated loss at $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, well above the moist lowlands ($$47$$), the eastern escarpment ($$37$$) and the dry lowlands ($$6$$), confirming the highlands as the most erosion-prone region.

**State the agricultural consequences.** The table lists exposed plant roots, severe yield reduction and loss of topsoil for the highlands. The unit adds that erosion depletes nitrogen and phosphorus, lowers water retention capacity, reduces soil depth and exposes roots, making crops highly vulnerable to drought.

questions.q:
A soil conservation team compares two Eritrean sites using the unit's regional soil-loss figures. Site A is highland farmland whose measured loss falls at the lower end of the highland range given in the unit ($$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). Site B is dry lowland farmland losing $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
(a) Calculate how many times greater the soil loss at Site A is than at Site B.
(b) The unit also notes that under natural conditions $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ of fertile topsoil takes $$100\text{ to }400\text{ years}$$ to form, and that a loss of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year represents approximately $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate. Using the mid-point of the formation range ($$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter), calculate the average annual topsoil formation in millimetres per year, and hence explain in one sentence how Site A's loss compares with it.
questions.answer: (a) Site A ($$50\text{ tons/ha/year}$$) loses about $$8.3\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Site B ($$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). (b) Using the mid-point of $$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter, natural topsoil formation averages $$0.04\text{ mm per year}$$, so Site A's loss of roughly $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year is about $$100\text{ times}$$ faster than the soil can be replaced.
why: **Extract the soil-loss figures for the two sites.** The unit table gives the highlands an estimated soil loss of $$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$ and the dry lowlands $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$. Site A lies at the lower end of the highland range, so its loss is $$50\text{ tons/ha/year}$$; Site B loses $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
**State the ratio to be computed.** The required comparison is a ratio: $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{\text{Loss at Site A}}{\text{Loss at Site B}}$$.
**Substitute and carry out the division.** $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{50}{6} = 8.33$$, i.e. approximately $$8.3\text{ times}$$.

**Convert the natural formation range into an annual rate.** Under natural conditions $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ ($$= 10\text{ mm}$$) of topsoil needs $$100\text{ to }400\text{ years}$$. Taking the mid-point of $$250\text{ years}$$ per centimeter, the average annual formation is $$\dfrac{10\text{ mm}}{250\text{ years}} = 0.04\text{ mm per year}$$.

**Relate the computed loss rate to the formation rate.** The unit states that a loss of approximately $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil per year is about $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate. This is consistent with the computed formation rate: $$\dfrac{4\text{ mm}}{0.04\text{ mm per year}} = 100$$ - that is, at the lower-end highland loss of $$50\text{ t/ha/year}$$ the soil is still being removed many times faster than the $$0.04\text{ mm per year}$$ at which fertile topsoil forms naturally.

**State the agronomic consequence.** Because accumulation cannot keep pace with removal, the topsoil layer thins progressively. This matches the unit's description of land degradation as a continuous process marked by progressive weakening of the physical, chemical and biological potential of land, and of erosion causing nutrient depletion (especially nitrogen and phosphorus), lower water retention, reduced soil depth and exposed plant roots.

**Draw the conservation conclusion.** The comparison shows that Site A loses roughly $$8.3\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Site B, and still loses topsoil dozens of times faster than nature rebuilds it, so a physical or biological soil and water conservation measure - for example hillside terraces on the sloping highland plot - is required rather than relying on natural soil formation.

questions.q:
Two farms are compared using the unit's regional figures. Farm X lies in the highlands, where the measured soil loss is at the upper end of the unit's highland range ($$50 - 100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$). Farm Y lies in the dry lowlands, where the primary causative agent is wind and the estimated loss is $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
(a) Calculate the ratio of Farm X's soil loss to Farm Y's.
(b) Using the unit figure of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil lost per year at the mean steep-slope loss rate, and a natural formation time of $$100\text{ years}$$ for $$1\text{ centimeter}$$ of topsoil, calculate the annual natural formation rate and state how many times larger the loss rate is.
questions.answer: (a) $$\dfrac{100}{6} = 16.7$$, so about $$16.7\text{ times}$$ (roughly $$17\text{ times}$$). (b) $$\dfrac{10\text{ mm}}{100\text{ years}} = 0.1\text{ mm per year}$$, so the $$4\text{ mm per year}$$ loss is $$40\text{ times}$$ the natural formation rate
why: **Read the required values from the unit.** The upper end of the highland range is $$100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, so Farm X loses $$100\text{ tons/ha/year}$$; the dry lowland figure is $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$, so Farm Y loses $$6\text{ tons/ha/year}$$.
**Compute the ratio.** $$\text{Ratio} = \dfrac{100}{6} = 16.7$$, so Farm X loses about $$16.7\text{ times}$$ as much soil as Farm Y.
**Convert formation time to an annual rate.** $$1\text{ centimeter} = 10\text{ mm}$$ forms in $$100\text{ years}$$, so the natural formation rate is $$\dfrac{10}{100} = 0.1\text{ mm per year}$$.

**Compare loss with formation.** $$\dfrac{4\text{ mm per year}}{0.1\text{ mm per year}} = 40$$, so the loss rate is $$40\text{ times}$$ the natural formation rate at the fastest possible natural formation.

**Interpret the result.** Even under the most favourable natural soil-building conditions in the unit ($$100\text{ years}$$ per centimeter), erosion on steep highland farmland removes topsoil far faster than it forms, which is why the unit calls topsoil a precious, slow-forming resource and why conservation measures are indispensable.

questions.q:
A highland catchment of $$200\text{ hectares}$$ is losing topsoil by water erosion at the unit's mean rate for steep slopes of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$.
(a) Calculate the total annual soil loss from the catchment in tons.
(b) Given that this mean rate corresponds to an annual loss of approximately $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil, calculate the total volume of topsoil lost each year in cubic metres (take $$1\text{ m}^3$$ of topsoil $$= 1.3\text{ tons}$$), and express your answer to the nearest whole cubic metre.
(c) State one conservation measure from the unit that would directly reduce this loss on the sloping cultivated land, and one that would trap the sediment already being carried away.
questions.answer: (a) $$200 \times 42 = 8\,400\text{ tons per year}$$. (b) $$\dfrac{8\,400}{1.3} = 6\,461.5$$, so approximately $$6\,462\text{ m}^3$$ of topsoil per year. (c) Hillside terraces (or contour bunds) on the sloping cultivated land reduce detachment and runoff, while check dams built across active gullies trap the sediment and slow the water.
why: **Identify the mean loss rate and area.** The unit reports a mean soil loss of $$42\text{ tons per hectare per year}$$ on steep slopes, and the catchment area is $$200\text{ hectares}$$.
**Compute the total annual soil loss.** $$\text{Total loss} = 42\text{ tons/ha/year} \times 200\text{ ha} = 8\,400\text{ tons per year}$$.

**Convert tons of soil to volume.** Using $$1\text{ m}^3 = 1.3\text{ tons}$$, the volume is $$\dfrac{8\,400\text{ tons}}{1.3\text{ tons/m}^3} = 6\,461.5\text{ m}^3$$, which rounds to approximately $$6\,462\text{ m}^3$$ per year.

**Link the loss to the thinning topsoil layer.** The unit notes that the mean steep-slope loss represents an annual loss of about $$4\text{ mm}$$ of topsoil, roughly $$20\text{ times}$$ the possible soil replacement rate, so this volume represents a layer of fertile topsoil that natural formation cannot replace within a human lifetime.

**Select measures that reduce and trap the loss.** Hillside terraces are a physical measure that breaks slope length and traps water and sediment on sloping cultivated hills, and contour bunds intercept surface runoff and encourage infiltration on gently sloping croplands. Check dams are built across gullies to slow water velocity and trap sediment, preventing the gullies from widening.

cards.title: 4.1.1 Agriculture and the Farm
body: Agriculture can be defined as an industry involving the organization of resources such as land, capital, labour and management for the production of food and non-food agricultural products.

cards.title: 4.1.2 The Importance of Farm Management
body: The term “farm management” comprises two words: “farm” and “management”.
A “farm” includes all the land on which a person performs some kind of agricultural operation, either by his/her own labour or family labour or hired employees.

“Management”, on the other hand, is the function of combining ideas, physical and human resources, and processing these efficiently to achieve stated objectives such as an increase in the productivity of farm output, or the profitability of the farm.
In commercial farms, the main objective is the maximization of profit of the farm or the minimization of the cost of production.

cards.title: 4.1.3 Agriculture as Industry
body: People work in different activities such as in teaching, providing health services, production of crops, shoes, clothing and in raising livestock, etc.
With economic development, agriculture has taken on a broader meaning.
Additionally, a good knowledge of the interrelationship between agriculture, the environment and sustainable development is crucial.
**Agriculture** is the most important industry in developing countries.

cards.title: 4.1.4 Factors of Production
body: **Economics** is the study of how people allocate their limited resources in order to satisfy their unlimited wants over time.
Land: This is the most important factor of production for a farmer.
A farmer must have land to grow food or raise livestock.
Labour: This is the productive contribution of humans who work, both mentally and physically, on the farm.

cards.title: 4.1.5 Basic Economic Principles
body: The relationship between inputs and outputs can be described as a production function.

The production function is thus a technical and mathematical relationship describing the manner and extent to which a particular product depends upon the quantities of input(s) or services of inputs used under a given state of technology.
Production functions can be expressed in three forms: tabular, graphic and algebraic.
Where y represents a dependent variable, such as crop yield, and x represents an independent variable, such as fertiliser, with ƒ denoting “function of”.

cards.q: Under what conditions is a farm said to be insolvent or bankrupt on its balance sheet?

options.A: When total revenues are lower than variable costs.
options.B: When net worth or owner's equity is negative.
options.C: When current assets exceed long-term liabilities.
options.D: When there is a net loss on the income statement.
options.E: When no physical inventory is kept.

cards.why:
**Reasoning**
A balance sheet reflects the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Net worth (owner's equity) is calculated as Assets minus Liabilities. If a farm's total liabilities (debts) exceed its total assets, the net worth becomes negative, which means the farm is insolvent or bankrupt.

**Conclusion**
Therefore, insolvency occurs **When net worth or owner's equity is negative**.

cards.title: 4.2.1 Farm Accounting Records
body: **An inventory** is a statement in which all the physical assets of the farm business and their monetary values are recorded.
The inventory should be prepared at least once a year.
When physically measuring assets, numbers and quantities should be established i.e. how many hectares of land, livestock, bags of grain, machinery and equipment, etc.
In order to calculate the monetary values of assets, all the physical assets should be valued and depreciation deducted.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Physical Production, Labour and Machinery Records
body: Production records are valuable to diagnose problems and identify opportunities for business.
The statements most commonly used are crop cultivation, livestock, labour and machinery statements.
Crop cultivation statements contain information on a specific crop or type of fruit that is being cultivated.
The various field or orchard numbers, areas, yield potential and soil analysis of the land used for cultivating that particular crop or fruit are recorded.

cards.title: 4.2.3 Financial Statements
body: A full set of financial statements would consist of a balance sheet, an income statement and a cash-flow statement.
**A balance sheet** is a financial statement which reflects the financial position of a farm business on a specific date (at a specific moment in time).
The relations of assets, liabilities and capital represent the financial position of farm enterprises.
**The balance sheet** is the systematic presentation of these three aspects for a specific date, with each individual item being identified and linked to a monetary value.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In a classical agricultural production function, which stage of production represents the 'rational zone' where the profit-maximizing input level is located?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Stage I is a zone of under-utilization where input efficiency is still rising. Stage III is a zone of waste where adding more inputs decreases total product (negative MP). Stage II is the only rational zone of production because the marginal product is positive but decreasing, and the optimal profit-maximizing point (where MVP = Px) lies within its boundaries.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the rational zone is **Stage II**.

cards.title: 4.3.1 Planning
body: Farm planning is fundamental to the management process, because farming has become a complex business.

Labour: : Labour needed for particular farm operations must be assessed for the farming season (specific months or year).
As labour is heterogeneous, the total labour required is estimated based on person-days.

cards.title: 4.3.2 Decision-making
body: The main objective of farm planning and budgeting is to make better decisions.
